title: Organic Chemistry of Biomolecules
summary: Apply organic structure and reactivity to sugars, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates: Ring Forms, Anomers and Glycosidic Bonds

levels.kid:
Sugar molecules are like little chains of carbon atoms. But in water, most sugars like to curl up and bite their own tail, making a **ring**. Glucose, the sugar your brain runs on, makes a ring with six corners.

When the ring closes, one special spot can point either up or down. Chemists give these two shapes different names, like twins who look almost the same but part their hair on different sides.

Sugars can also hold hands. When two sugar rings join, the link is called a **glycosidic bond**. Long chains of glucose make **starch** in bread and potatoes. A different way of linking makes **cellulose**, the tough stuff in plants. Same building blocks, different links, very different foods!
levels.hs:
**Carbohydrates** are sugars and the molecules built from them. A simple sugar like **glucose** (C6H12O6) has a carbonyl group (C=O) and several hydroxyl groups (-OH).

In water, glucose rarely stays as a straight chain. The -OH on carbon 5 attacks the carbonyl carbon (carbon 1), closing a six-membered ring called a **pyranose**. This new structure is a **hemiacetal**: one carbon attached to both an -OH and a ring oxygen. Fructose often forms a five-membered ring called a **furanose**.

Closing the ring creates a new stereocenter at carbon 1, called the **anomeric carbon**. Its -OH can point two ways:
- **alpha (α)**: opposite side from the CH2OH group (drawn down)
- **beta (β)**: same side (drawn up)

The two forms, called **anomers**, interconvert in water through the open chain. This is **mutarotation**. At equilibrium glucose is about 64% β and 36% α, with less than 1% open chain.

When the anomeric -OH reacts with an -OH on another sugar, it forms a **glycosidic bond**. Table sugar (sucrose) is glucose linked to fructose. Real example: **starch** uses α(1→4) links that humans digest easily, while **cellulose** uses β(1→4) links. We lack an enzyme to break those, so cellulose passes through us as fiber.
levels.college:
**Cyclization.** Aldoses and ketoses undergo intramolecular nucleophilic addition: a hydroxyl oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon to give a cyclic **hemiacetal** (from aldehydes) or **hemiketal** (from ketones). Five- and six-membered rings are favored because they have low ring strain and a high effective molarity. D-glucose uses O5 to give a pyranose. D-fructose's keto C2 is attacked by O5 to give a furanose (or by O6 to give a pyranose).

**Anomers.** C1 of an aldose becomes a new stereocenter. The two epimers at this carbon are anomers.
- In the D-series Haworth projection, α has the anomeric OH trans to C6 (down), and β has it cis (up).
- In the ⁴C₁ chair of β-D-glucopyranose, every bulky substituent is equatorial. This helps explain why β dominates (~64%) and why glucose is the most abundant monosaccharide in nature.
- Mutarotation is acid- or base-catalyzed ring opening and reclosure. Specific rotation drifts from +112° (pure α) or +19° (pure β) toward +52.7°.

**Reducing sugars.** A free hemiacetal is in equilibrium with an open-chain aldehyde, which can reduce Cu²⁺ (Benedict's test). This open-chain aldehyde is also the reactive species in nonenzymatic **glycation**.

**Glycosides.** Under acid catalysis, a hemiacetal reacts with an alcohol to form an **acetal**, called a glycoside. Acetals are stable to base and do not mutarotate. Their configuration is locked as α or β.
- Maltose: Glc α(1→4) Glc (reducing)
- Lactose: Gal β(1→4) Glc (reducing)
- Sucrose: Glc α1↔β2 Fru (non-reducing; both anomeric carbons are tied up)
- Glycogen: α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches

N-glycosides link sugars to nitrogen, for example the Asn-linked glycans of glycoproteins.
levels.phd:
**The anomeric effect.** Simple sterics predict equatorial substituents, yet electronegative anomeric groups prefer the axial position more than sterics alone allow. Glucose is 36% α even though its α-OH is axial. In methyl glycosides and glycosyl halides, the axial preference becomes dominant. The leading explanation is hyperconjugation: a lone pair on the ring oxygen donates into the antibonding σ*(C1–X) orbital, and this donation works best when the two are antiperiplanar, which occurs with axial X. Dipole minimization also contributes. The relative weight of these two factors is still debated, and computational work (e.g., Mo's block-localized analyses) has argued that electrostatics are underrated. Edward and Lemieux defined the effect in the 1950s.

**Glycosidic bond formation and cleavage.** Acid hydrolysis proceeds through protonation of the exocyclic oxygen and departure of the aglycone. This generates an **oxocarbenium ion**: C1 becomes sp²-like and the ring flattens to a half-chair. Chemical glycosylation runs this pathway in reverse. Its stereochemical outcome is controlled by:
- neighboring-group participation (a C2 ester forms a dioxolenium ion, giving 1,2-trans products)
- solvent effects (nitrile solvents favor β)
- leaving group and promoter choice

The 1,2-cis linkages, such as β-mannosides, are notoriously hard to make. Crich's 4,6-benzylidene triflate method is a classic solution.

**Enzymatic hydrolysis.** Koshland (1953) classified glycosidases into two types:
- **Retaining** enzymes use a double displacement. A carboxylate nucleophile forms a covalent glycosyl-enzyme intermediate, and a second carboxylate acts as acid/base. The two carboxylates sit about 5.5 Å apart.
- **Inverting** enzymes use a single displacement. A water molecule is activated between carboxylates about 10 Å apart.

Withers trapped the covalent intermediates with 2-fluoro sugars, which destabilize the oxocarbenium-like transition states. Hen egg-white lysozyme was shown to be retaining-covalent, overturning Phillips' original ion-pair proposal.

The α versus β linkage determines macromolecular form. Starch amylose coils into helices, whereas cellulose forms flat ribbons that hydrogen-bond into crystalline microfibrils.
levels.expert:
**Transition-state mimicry in pharmacology.** Glycosidase inhibitors mimic the flattened, positively charged oxocarbenium transition state.
- **Acarbose** (a pseudotetrasaccharide) and **miglitol** (an iminosugar) inhibit intestinal α-glucosidases to blunt the rise in blood glucose after meals.
- **Oseltamivir** and **zanamivir** mimic the half-chair sialyl cation in influenza neuraminidase, so new virions cannot release from sialic-acid receptors.
- **Miglustat** inhibits glucosylceramide synthase (substrate reduction therapy) in Gaucher disease. Related iminosugars act as pharmacological chaperones for misfolded lysosomal enzymes.

**Glycosides as drug architecture.** Digoxin's trisdigitoxose chain, the aminoglycosides (gentamicin), macrolide desosamine and the anthracyclines all depend on specific glycosidic stereochemistry for target binding. SGLT2 inhibitors such as **dapagliflozin** are **C-glycosides**. Replacing O with C at the anomeric position resists glycosidase hydrolysis, which gives oral stability. Many natural products are prodrugs whose glycosides are cleaved by gut bacteria. Sennosides and the conversion of the glucuronide conjugates of morphine are examples. Glucuronidation itself installs a β-glycosidic (acetal) linkage during phase II metabolism. Acyl glucuronides, however, are esters that can undergo acyl migration and covalently modify proteins, a known toxicity signal.

**Clinical chemistry pitfalls.**
- HbA1c reflects Amadori products formed from glucose's minor open-chain form. Hemoglobin variants and altered red cell lifespan (hemolysis, transfusion, CKD) distort it.
- Galactose, xylose and maltose (from icodextrin dialysate) cross-react with some glucose-dehydrogenase PQQ meters, causing falsely high readings.

**Neuro relevance.** Polysialic acid on NCAM governs neural plasticity. Hyaluronan and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans form perineuronal nets and glial scar. Chondroitinase ABC, which degrades glycosaminoglycan chains, promotes axon regrowth in spinal cord injury models.

**Frontiers.** Automated glycan assembly (Seeberger) and one-pot programmable glycosylation are making carbohydrate synthesis more routine. Engineered glycosynthases are mutant retaining enzymes that lack the nucleophile and use glycosyl fluorides as donors. Precise control of the 1,2-cis linkage and the rules of the glycan code remain open questions.

keyPoints: Sugars cyclize by intramolecular attack of an OH on the carbonyl, forming hemiacetals
Six-membered rings are pyranoses; five-membered rings are furanoses
The anomeric carbon (C1 of aldoses) gives α and β anomers
Mutarotation interconverts anomers via the open chain; glucose is ~64% β
Glycosidic bonds are acetals that lock the anomeric configuration
α(1→4) starch is digestible; β(1→4) cellulose is not

test.q: When glucose closes into a ring, which functional group forms?
test.explain: An OH adding to an aldehyde carbonyl gives a hemiacetal: one carbon bearing an OH and an OR.

test.q: A six-membered sugar ring containing one oxygen is called a:
test.explain: The pyranose ring is named after pyran; furanoses are five-membered.

test.q: Which carbon of glucose becomes the anomeric carbon?
test.explain: The aldehyde carbon C1 becomes a new stereocenter on ring closure. C5 supplies the attacking oxygen.

test.q: What is mutarotation?
choices: Enzymatic conversion of glucose into fructose
Anomers interconverting via the open chain
Flipping between D and L forms of a sugar
Free rotation about a glycosidic bond
test.explain: The ring opens and recloses, letting α and β interconvert. D and L do not interconvert this way.

test.q: Why is β-D-glucopyranose the major anomer in water?
test.explain: In the chair, every bulky substituent of the β anomer is equatorial, minimizing steric strain.

test.q: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar?
choices: It is made of two glucose units
Both anomeric carbons are in the link
Its rings are too large to open
test.explain: The Glc α1↔β2 Fru link ties up both anomeric carbons, so neither ring can open to a free carbonyl.

test.q: Humans cannot digest cellulose mainly because it has:
test.explain: Human enzymes cleave α(1→4) starch links but not the β(1→4) links of cellulose.

test.q: Glycogen's branch points use which linkage?
test.explain: Glycogen has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches.

test.q: Unlike a hemiacetal, a glycoside (acetal):
test.explain: Acetals are base-stable and do not open, so α or β is locked.

test.q: The two stereoisomers that differ only at the anomeric carbon are called ___.
test.explain: α and β forms are anomers, a special type of epimer.

test.q: What is the five-membered sugar ring form (common for fructose) called?
test.explain: It is named after furan, a five-membered ring with one oxygen.

test.q: The bond joining two sugars through the anomeric carbon is a ___ bond.
test.explain: Glycosidic bonds are acetal linkages between sugars or other groups.

kidTest.q: What shape do most sugars make in water?
kidTest.explain: Sugars curl up and join their own ends to make a ring.

kidTest.q: How many corners does a glucose ring have?
kidTest.explain: Glucose makes a six-cornered ring.

kidTest.q: What is the link between two sugars called?
kidTest.explain: Sugars join with glycosidic bonds.

kidTest.q: Which food is made of long chains of glucose that we digest?
kidTest.explain: Starch in bread and potatoes is a glucose chain.

kidTest.q: The tough sugar chain in plants that we cannot digest: c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Cellulose uses a different link that our bodies cannot break.

advancedTest.q: Glucose is 36% α even though its α-OH is axial. The best explanation is:
choices: Greater ring strain in the β chair conformation
Faster crystallization of the α anomer from water
Hydrogen bonding between the anomeric OH and C6 OH
Ring-oxygen lone pair donation into σ*(C1–O) when axial
advancedTest.explain: The anomeric effect: the antiperiplanar n→σ* overlap is best with an axial substituent, which offsets steric preference.

advancedTest.q: A glycosidase's two catalytic carboxylates sit about 10 Å apart. This suggests it:
choices: Inverts configuration via a single displacement
Retains configuration via a covalent intermediate
Cleaves C-glycosides as easily as O-glycosides
advancedTest.explain: A wide gap accommodates water between the carboxylates for direct attack (inversion). Retaining enzymes have about 5.5 Å spacing.

advancedTest.q: A C2 ester protecting group on a glycosyl donor tends to give 1,2-trans products because:
choices: It makes C1 a much better nucleophile
It forms a dioxolenium ion blocking one face
It locks the donor into a furanose ring
advancedTest.explain: Neighboring-group participation forms a bridged ion, so the acceptor attacks from the opposite face.

advancedTest.q: Why are SGLT2 inhibitors like dapagliflozin built as C-glycosides?
choices: They form oxocarbenium ions more readily in the gut
Carbon allows mutarotation to the active anomer
They resist glycosidase hydrolysis, aiding oral stability
C–C anomeric bonds make them reducing sugars
advancedTest.explain: Replacing the anomeric O with C removes the acetal that glycosidases cleave, so the drug survives the gut and circulation.

lessons.title: Amino Acid Side-Chain Reactivity and the Peptide Bond

levels.kid:
Proteins are like long necklaces made of beads. Each bead is an **amino acid**. There are 20 kinds of beads in your body's protein kit.

Every bead has the same middle part, but each one has its own little "tail" sticking out. Some tails love water. Some tails hide from water, like oil does. Some tails are sticky with a tiny electric charge. One tail, on a bead called cysteine, can grab another cysteine and lock on like a clasp.

The string that joins the beads is called the **peptide bond**. It is very strong and flat, like a stiff little plank. Because the tails are all different, the necklace folds into a special shape, and that shape lets the protein do its job.
levels.hs:
Proteins are chains of **amino acids**. Each amino acid has a central carbon (the alpha carbon) attached to an **amino group** (–NH2), a **carboxyl group** (–COOH), a hydrogen, and a **side chain** (the R group). The side chain is what makes each of the 20 standard amino acids different.

Side chains fall into groups:
- **Nonpolar** (like leucine and valine): oily, they cluster inside proteins away from water.
- **Polar** (like serine and asparagine): they form hydrogen bonds with water.
- **Acidic** (aspartate, glutamate): negatively charged at body pH.
- **Basic** (lysine, arginine): positively charged at body pH.
- **Cysteine**: its –SH group can pair with another cysteine to form a **disulfide bond**, a covalent bridge that holds proteins together.

Amino acids join through a **peptide bond**, an amide formed between one amino acid's carboxyl group and the next one's amino group, releasing water. This is a condensation reaction. The chain has a direction: an **N-terminus** at one end and a **C-terminus** at the other.

A real example: insulin is made of two chains held together by disulfide bonds. Breaking those bonds destroys insulin's activity, showing how side-chain chemistry controls a protein's shape and function.
levels.college:
Each alpha-amino acid (except glycine) has a stereocenter at the alpha carbon; proteins use the **L** configuration, which is **S** for all except cysteine (R, because sulfur raises the CIP priority of its side chain). At physiological pH (~7.4) free amino acids exist as **zwitterions** (–NH3+ and –COO−).

**Side-chain acid–base chemistry** (approximate free amino acid pKa values):
- Asp ~3.9, Glu ~4.1: carboxylates at pH 7.4.
- His ~6.0: imidazole near neutral pH, so it shuttles protons in enzymes (e.g., the catalytic triad of chymotrypsin).
- Cys ~8.3: thiol, partly ionized; thiolate is a strong nucleophile.
- Tyr ~10.1, Lys ~10.5, Arg ~12.5: mostly protonated at pH 7.4.

**Nucleophilic side chains**: Ser and Thr hydroxyls, the Cys thiol, the Lys ε-amine, and His imidazole attack electrophiles. Serine proteases use an activated Ser–OH; many drugs exploit this. Aspirin acetylates a serine (Ser530) in cyclooxygenase, irreversibly blocking it.

**Redox**: two Cys thiols oxidize to a **disulfide** (cystine), stabilizing extracellular proteins such as antibodies and insulin. Reducing agents (dithiothreitol, glutathione) reverse it.

**The peptide bond** is an amide. Nitrogen's lone pair delocalizes into the carbonyl, so:
- The C–N bond has ~40% double-bond character and is shorter (~1.33 Å) than a typical C–N single bond (~1.47 Å).
- The six atoms around it are **planar**, and rotation is restricted; most peptide bonds are **trans**.
- Resonance makes the carbonyl a poor electrophile, so uncatalyzed hydrolysis is extremely slow. Proteases are needed to cut it.

Forming the bond needs activation. Cells activate amino acids as aminoacyl-tRNA esters; chemists use coupling reagents such as carbodiimides.
levels.phd:
Amide resonance underlies much of protein chemistry. Delocalization (resonance stabilization roughly 15–20 kcal/mol) gives a rotational barrier around ~20 kcal/mol, locking ω near 180°. Backbone flexibility therefore resides in φ and ψ, the torsions Ramachandran mapped from steric clashes. **Proline** is the exception: its tertiary amide makes cis and trans prolyl bonds close in energy (~5–30% cis in unfolded peptides). Their slow interconversion can limit folding rates and is catalyzed by peptidyl-prolyl isomerases (cyclophilin, FKBP), the targets of cyclosporin and tacrolimus.

Uncatalyzed peptide hydrolysis at neutral pH has a half-life on the order of hundreds of years (Smith and Hansen estimated ~350–600 years). Serine proteases achieve enormous rate enhancements using a Ser–His–Asp triad. The Asp orients His, which acts as a general base to activate Ser195. Ser195 attacks to form a tetrahedral intermediate stabilized by the **oxyanion hole**, then an acyl-enzyme, which is hydrolyzed.

**Side-chain pKa values are environment-dependent.** Burial in a low-dielectric interior, nearby charges and hydrogen bonds shift pKa by several units. Examples include the Lys of acetoacetate decarboxylase (pKa ~6, Westheimer), which forms a Schiff base, and active-site cysteines with pKa values near 3–4 stabilized by helix dipoles and His ion pairs. Reactivity thus depends on microenvironment rather than textbook values.

**Cysteine chemistry** is the most versatile: thiolate nucleophilicity, disulfide exchange (thiol–disulfide interchange via SN2 at sulfur), and oxidation to sulfenic, sulfinic and sulfonic acids in redox signaling. Disulfide formation in the ER is catalyzed by protein disulfide isomerase.

**Spontaneous side-chain chemistry** matters too. Asparagine **deamidation**, especially at Asn–Gly sequences, proceeds through backbone nitrogen attack forming a succinimide. The succinimide hydrolyzes to Asp and isoAsp, adding a negative charge and kinking the backbone. Deamidation acts as a molecular clock in long-lived proteins like lens crystallins, and is repaired partly by PIMT (protein L-isoaspartyl methyltransferase).
levels.expert:
Side-chain reactivity now drives drug design. **Targeted covalent inhibitors** place a mild electrophile, typically an acrylamide Michael acceptor, near a non-catalytic cysteine. Ibrutinib binds Cys481 of Bruton's tyrosine kinase, osimertinib binds Cys797 of EGFR, and sotorasib and adagrasib bind the mutant Cys12 of KRAS G12C, a target long called "undruggable." Potency combines reversible affinity (Ki) with the inactivation rate constant (kinact), so kinact/KI, not IC50, is the correct metric. Resistance arises predictably: EGFR C797S and BTK C481S remove the thiol. Newer warheads target lysine and tyrosine using sulfonyl fluorides and related electrophiles, and chemoproteomic profiling (activity-based protein profiling, isoTOP-ABPP of Cravatt and colleagues) maps ligandable cysteines across the proteome.

In **biologics**, side-chain liabilities set shelf life. Development teams screen antibody sequences for Asn–Gly and Asn–Ser deamidation hotspots, Asp–Gly isomerization, Met and Trp oxidation, and free cysteines that cause scrambled disulfides or aggregation. Mutating these residues is routine. Neurosurgically relevant: isoAsp and other aging modifications accumulate in long-lived amyloid-β and tau and may influence aggregation, although causality remains debated.

**Peptide therapeutics** fight the backbone's vulnerability to proteases. Strategies include D-amino acids, N-methylation (which also improves membrane permeability, as in cyclosporin), cyclization, and α-methyl residues. Semaglutide's Aib at position 2 resists DPP-4 cleavage, and lipidation extends its half-life through albumin binding.

**Synthesis**: Merrifield's solid-phase peptide synthesis (Nobel 1984) with Fmoc chemistry dominates. Racemization via oxazolone formation during carboxyl activation is the key pitfall, suppressed by additives such as HOBt or Oxyma. Native chemical ligation (Kent) joins unprotected segments: a C-terminal thioester undergoes transthioesterification with an N-terminal Cys, then an S→N acyl shift forms a native peptide bond. Bioconjugation for antibody–drug conjugates exploits Cys–maleimide or Lys acylation, though maleimide adducts can undergo retro-Michael exchange with albumin. Open questions include predicting the pKa of buried residues accurately and designing selective covalent warheads for residues beyond cysteine.

keyPoints: Amino acids share a backbone; the side chain (R group) sets their chemistry
Side chains are nonpolar, polar, acidic or basic; His pKa near 6 suits proton transfer
Ser, Cys, Lys and His side chains act as nucleophiles in enzymes and drug binding
Two cysteines oxidize to a disulfide bond that stabilizes protein structure
The peptide bond is a planar, resonance-stabilized amide, mostly trans
Amide resonance makes peptide hydrolysis very slow without proteases

test.q: Which amino acid side chain has a pKa near 6, making it useful for proton transfer in enzymes?
test.explain: Histidine's imidazole has a pKa of about 6, so it can gain or lose a proton near physiological pH. Lysine and arginine stay protonated, and aspartate stays deprotonated.

test.q: Why does the peptide bond resist rotation?
choices: Hydrogen bonds lock the alpha carbon
It is an ionic bond between charges
test.explain: Delocalization of nitrogen's lone pair into the carbonyl gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, making the amide planar.

test.q: A disulfide bond forms by oxidation of two side chains of which amino acid?
test.explain: Two cysteine thiols (–SH) oxidize to form an S–S bridge (cystine). Methionine contains sulfur but has no free thiol.

test.q: Forming a peptide bond from two amino acids releases which molecule?
test.explain: Peptide bond formation is a condensation reaction: an amide forms and water is lost.

test.q: Which group of side chains tends to cluster in a protein's interior?
test.explain: Nonpolar side chains avoid water and pack inside folded proteins, while charged and polar ones usually face the solvent.

test.q: Aspirin irreversibly blocks cyclooxygenase by acetylating which residue?
test.explain: Aspirin transfers its acetyl group to Ser530 of cyclooxygenase, a covalent and irreversible modification.

test.q: Why is uncatalyzed peptide bond hydrolysis so slow?
choices: Peptide bonds mostly adopt the strained cis form
Resonance makes the carbonyl a poor electrophile
Water rarely reaches the tightly packed backbone
The amide nitrogen is strongly basic and protonated
test.explain: Nitrogen's lone pair donates into the carbonyl, reducing its electrophilicity, so water attacks it very slowly without a protease. Peptide bonds are mostly trans, not cis.

test.q: At physiological pH, a free amino acid exists mainly as a:
test.explain: At pH ~7.4 the amino group is protonated (–NH3+) and the carboxyl is deprotonated (–COO−), giving a zwitterion.

test.q: Which statement about the peptide bond's geometry is correct?
choices: It rotates freely like an alkane
It is usually trans and planar
It is usually cis and bent
test.explain: The peptide bond is planar due to resonance and is overwhelmingly trans, which avoids steric clashes between neighboring residues.

test.q: The end of a protein chain with a free amino group is called the ___.
test.explain: Chains run from the N-terminus (free amine) to the C-terminus (free carboxyl).

test.q: What is the side chain of an amino acid often called, using a single letter?
test.explain: The side chain is called the R group, and it differs among the 20 amino acids.

test.q: Proteins use amino acids of the ___ configuration.
test.explain: Protein amino acids are L, which is S in CIP terms for all except cysteine.

kidTest.q: What are the beads in a protein necklace called?
kidTest.explain: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

kidTest.q: What makes each amino acid different?
kidTest.explain: Every amino acid has the same middle part but a different tail.

kidTest.q: What does the peptide bond do?
kidTest.explain: The peptide bond is the strong link between amino acids.

kidTest.q: Some tails hide from water. What are they like?
kidTest.explain: Oily tails stay away from water, just as oil does.

kidTest.q: Which bead can lock onto another one like a clasp? c _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Two cysteines can join to make a strong bridge.

advancedTest.q: An active-site cysteine has a pKa near 3.5 instead of the usual ~8.3. What best explains this and its consequence?
choices: Nearby positive charges stabilize thiolate, raising its nucleophilicity
High solvent exposure lowers the pKa and favors the neutral thiol form
Burial in oil lowers the pKa, making the thiol less reactive
Disulfide formation lowers the pKa and prevents nucleophilic attack
advancedTest.explain: Helix dipoles and His ion pairs stabilize the thiolate anion, lowering the pKa so the residue is ionized and highly nucleophilic at neutral pH.

advancedTest.q: Why are prolyl bonds a common rate-limiting step in protein folding?
choices: Proline side chains form disulfide bonds during folding
Proline is a secondary amide with a high cis preference
Proline peptide bonds form solely through enzyme catalysis
Cis and trans forms are close in energy but interconvert slowly
advancedTest.explain: As a tertiary amide, the prolyl bond has a small cis–trans energy gap but a high rotational barrier, so slow isomerization limits folding; isomerases speed it up.

advancedTest.q: A KRAS G12C covalent inhibitor loses activity in a resistant tumor with a second mutation. Which change most directly explains loss of covalent binding?
choices: Increased expression of albumin that binds the drug
Formation of an isoAsp residue at Asn–Gly sites
Replacement of the target thiol by a nonnucleophilic residue
Higher kinact due to a more reactive cysteine
advancedTest.explain: Covalent drugs need the nucleophilic thiol; mutations like EGFR C797S remove it. A higher kinact would improve, not abolish, binding.

advancedTest.q: Why does Asn deamidation occur fastest at Asn–Gly sequences?
choices: Glycine's flexibility lets its backbone N attack, forming a succinimide
Glycine donates a thiol that cleaves the asparagine amide
Glycine raises the pH locally, causing direct hydrolysis
Glycine's side chain is acidic and protonates the amide
advancedTest.explain: Glycine has no side chain to block the following residue's backbone nitrogen, which attacks the Asn side-chain amide to form the succinimide intermediate.

lessons.title: Lipids: Fatty Acid Esters, Unsaturation and the Steroid Nucleus

levels.kid:
Lipids are the body's fats and oils. They do not mix with water, just like oil floats on top of soup.

Many lipids are built from **fatty acids**. A fatty acid is a long chain of carbon atoms, like a long tail. Some tails are straight. Others have a bend in them. Straight tails stack neatly, like pencils in a box, so they make solid fats such as butter. Bent tails cannot stack well, so they make runny oils such as olive oil.

The body hooks three tails onto a small handle to store energy. That makes a fat molecule.

Another kind of lipid is a **steroid**. It looks like four rings stuck together. Cholesterol is a steroid. Your body uses it to make cell membranes and important messengers called hormones.
levels.hs:
**Lipids** are biomolecules defined by a property, not a single structure: they dissolve poorly in water but well in nonpolar solvents. That is because they are mostly carbon and hydrogen, which form nonpolar bonds.

Key lipid types:
- **Fatty acids**: a long hydrocarbon chain (usually 12-20 carbons, most often an even number) ending in a carboxylic acid group (-COOH). Palmitic acid has 16 carbons; stearic acid has 18.
- **Triglycerides** (triacylglycerols): three fatty acids joined to glycerol by **ester** bonds. An ester forms when an acid's -COOH joins an alcohol's -OH and water is released. Triglycerides are the body's main long-term energy store.
- **Steroids**: four fused carbon rings, such as cholesterol.

A **saturated** fatty acid has only C-C single bonds, so it holds the maximum number of hydrogens. An **unsaturated** fatty acid has one or more C=C double bonds. In natural fats these are usually **cis**, which puts a kink of about 30 degrees in the chain. Kinked chains cannot pack tightly, so they lower the melting point. That is why beef fat (more saturated) is solid at room temperature while olive oil (rich in oleic acid, 18 carbons with one cis double bond) is liquid.

Real example: industrial partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils created **trans fats**, which are straighter, pack like saturated fats, and raise LDL cholesterol. Many countries have now restricted or banned them.
levels.college:
**Fatty acid structure and naming.** Fatty acids are carboxylic acids with long unbranched chains. Shorthand gives chain length and number of double bonds: stearic 18:0, oleic 18:1 cis-Δ9, linoleic 18:2 cis-Δ9,12, α-linolenic 18:3 cis-Δ9,12,15. The **omega (n-) system** counts from the methyl end. Linoleic acid is ω-6 and α-linolenic acid is ω-3. Humans lack desaturases able to place double bonds beyond Δ9, so these two are **essential fatty acids**. Natural polyunsaturated acids are **methylene-interrupted**: their double bonds are separated by a CH2, so they are not conjugated. At physiological pH (pKa about 4.8, higher in membranes) fatty acids exist mainly as carboxylates.

**Physical consequences of unsaturation.**
- A cis double bond is rigid and introduces a kink. This disrupts van der Waals packing, so melting point falls (stearic about 69 °C, oleic about 13 °C).
- In membranes, unsaturated tails increase **fluidity**. Cholesterol buffers fluidity in both directions.

**Esters.** Triacylglycerols and glycerophospholipids are fatty acid esters of glycerol. Ester chemistry follows the acyl-transfer rules you met with carbonyls:
- **Saponification**: base hydrolysis gives glycerol plus carboxylate salts (soaps). It is irreversible because the carboxylate is deprotonated and no longer electrophilic.
- **Enzymatic hydrolysis**: lipases use a Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad. The serine is acylated, then the acyl-enzyme is hydrolysed.
- Biosynthesis does not use free acids. Cells activate fatty acids as **acyl-CoA thioesters**, which are better acyl donors than oxygen esters.

**Waxes** are esters of a fatty acid with a long-chain alcohol.

**The steroid nucleus.** Steroids share the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton: three six-membered rings (A, B, C) and one five-membered ring (D), with carbons numbered 1-17. Cholesterol (C27) has a 3β-OH group, a C5=C6 double bond, angular methyl groups C18 and C19, and an eight-carbon side chain at C17. Its trans ring fusions make a flat, rigid plate that slots between phospholipid tails.
levels.phd:
**Oxidative chemistry of unsaturation.** The bis-allylic CH2 between double bonds in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) has a C-H bond dissociation energy of roughly 75-80 kcal/mol, versus about 88 for a mono-allylic C-H and about 98-100 for an ordinary methylene. Abstraction gives a pentadienyl radical delocalized over five carbons. O2 adds at a terminus, creating a conjugated diene and a peroxyl radical, which then abstracts another bis-allylic H. This is the chain propagation of **lipid peroxidation**. Rates scale roughly with the number of bis-allylic positions, so docosahexaenoic acid (22:6) is far more oxidizable than linoleate. Breakdown products include the reactive aldehydes 4-hydroxynonenal and malondialdehyde. **α-Tocopherol** is a chain-breaking antioxidant: its phenolic O-H transfers H to the peroxyl radical, and the resulting stabilized tocopheroxyl radical is recycled by ascorbate.

**Enzymatic oxygenation.** Arachidonate (20:4 ω-6) is released from membrane phospholipids by cytosolic phospholipase A2. Cyclooxygenase (COX) then abstracts the 13-pro-S hydrogen using a tyrosyl radical (Tyr385) and inserts two O2 molecules, giving PGG2 and then PGH2. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates Ser530 of COX-1, an acyl transfer from a phenyl ester. Lipoxygenases use non-heme iron to make hydroperoxides regio- and stereoselectively.

**Steroid conformation.** Ring fusion stereochemistry defines shape. Cholesterol's B/C and C/D fusions are trans. 5α-Steroids (A/B trans) are nearly planar. 5β-Steroids such as the bile acids (A/B cis) are bent, which places their hydroxyls on one face and makes them **facially amphiphilic** detergents for micelles. Substituents are labelled β (same face as C18/C19 methyls) or α.

**Biosynthesis.** HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step to mevalonate, and statins inhibit it competitively. Isoprene (C5) units condense to squalene (C30). Squalene epoxidase forms 2,3-oxidosqualene, which lanosterol synthase folds in a chair-boat-chair conformation. Protonation of the epoxide triggers a cation-π-stabilized cascade that closes four rings, followed by sequential 1,2-hydride and methyl shifts. A single enzyme sets seven stereocentres. Cornforth, Bloch and Lynen shared this mechanistic history (Nobel Prizes 1964 and 1975).
levels.expert:
**Ferroptosis.** Ferroptosis is a regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent phospholipid peroxidation. ACSL4 preferentially converts arachidonic and adrenic acid to their CoA thioesters, which LPCAT3 then esterifies into phosphatidylethanolamine, enriching membranes with oxidizable substrate. GPX4, a selenoenzyme, reduces phospholipid hydroperoxides using glutathione. Inhibiting system xc- (with erastin) or GPX4 (with RSL3) triggers ferroptosis. FSP1 regenerates ubiquinol as a parallel radical-trapping antioxidant. Ferroptosis is studied in ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration and secondary injury after intracerebral haemorrhage, where heme iron is abundant. Ferrostatin-1 and liproxstatin-1 are research tools; clinical translation remains open.

**Isotope reinforcement.** Replacing the bis-allylic hydrogens of linoleate with deuterium (11,11-D2-linoleic acid) slows the rate-limiting H abstraction through a large kinetic isotope effect. This chemistry-to-clinic idea has been tested in Friedreich ataxia and other neurodegenerative diseases, with mixed results.

**Lipid-based drug design.**
- Ester prodrugs of steroids (for example, testosterone enanthate, estradiol valerate, betamethasone dipropionate) increase lipophilicity. They form an intramuscular depot or improve skin penetration, and tissue esterases release the active drug.
- Small structural changes switch steroid pharmacology. A 1,2-double bond plus 9α-fluorine and a 16α-methyl group (dexamethasone) boosts glucocorticoid potency and reduces mineralocorticoid activity. A 17α-ethynyl group (ethinylestradiol) blocks oxidation at C17 and makes the drug orally active.
- Lipid nanoparticles for mRNA use ionizable lipids, some with biodegradable ester linkers, plus cholesterol for packing.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Myelin is about 70-80% lipid by dry weight and very rich in cholesterol and plasmalogens, which carry a vinyl ether bond at sn-1. Brain cholesterol is made locally because lipoproteins do not cross the blood-brain barrier, and it is cleared as 24S-hydroxycholesterol (CYP46A1). Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (a DHCR7 defect, causing 7-dehydrocholesterol build-up) shows how a single missing step in the steroid pathway disturbs brain development. 7-Dehydrocholesterol is also highly oxidizable.

**Analytical pitfalls.** Samples oxidize ex vivo unless butylated hydroxytoluene is added. Isobaric species confound shotgun lipidomics. Simple shorthand such as "PC 34:1" hides positional isomers.

**Open questions.** Researchers are still asking how membrane PUFA content is matched to oxidative risk, and whether dietary ω-3 enrichment protects the brain or adds peroxidizable substrate.

keyPoints: Lipids are defined by poor water solubility, from nonpolar hydrocarbon chains
Triglycerides are glycerol triesters; saponification is irreversible base hydrolysis
Cis double bonds kink chains, lowering melting point and raising membrane fluidity
Linoleic (ω-6) and α-linolenic (ω-3) acids are essential
Weak bis-allylic C-H bonds make PUFAs prone to radical lipid peroxidation
Steroids share a rigid four-ring (6-6-6-5) nucleus; cholesterol is the parent sterol

lessons.title: Phosphate Esters and Anhydrides: The Chemistry of ATP

levels.kid:
Your body runs on a tiny molecule called **ATP**. Think of it like a phone battery that every cell uses.

ATP has a tail of three small groups called **phosphates**, lined up in a row. Each phosphate carries extra negative charge. Negative charges push each other away, like the same ends of two magnets. So the tail is a bit tense, like a stretched spring.

When the cell snaps off the last phosphate, the spring relaxes and energy is released. The cell uses that energy to move muscles, send nerve signals and build new things.

Then the cell sticks a phosphate back on to recharge the battery. You make and use about your own body weight in ATP every day!
levels.hs:
**Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)** is the main energy currency of cells. It has three parts: the base **adenine**, the sugar **ribose**, and a chain of three **phosphate groups**, labeled alpha (α), beta (β) and gamma (γ). The alpha phosphate is the one closest to the sugar.

Two kinds of bonds hold the phosphates on:
- A **phosphate ester** links the α-phosphate to an oxygen on ribose (P-O-C).
- **Phosphoanhydride bonds** link phosphate to phosphate (P-O-P). An anhydride forms when two acids join and lose water.

When water breaks the last anhydride bond, called **hydrolysis**, ATP becomes ADP plus inorganic phosphate (Pi). Under cell conditions this releases a lot of free energy, around -50 kJ/mol. Chemists sometimes call these bonds "high-energy," but the energy is not stored in one bond. It comes from the products being much more stable than ATP:
- Less crowding of negative charge
- Better resonance sharing of electrons in free phosphate
- Better hydration by water

Cells use this by **coupling**. They transfer a phosphate from ATP to another molecule so an uphill reaction can happen. For example, the enzyme hexokinase moves the γ-phosphate of ATP onto glucose. This traps glucose inside the cell and starts glycolysis.
levels.college:
Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) can form mono-, di- and triesters, and it can condense with itself to form anhydrides. In biology:
- **Phosphate monoesters**: sugar phosphates, phosphoserine in signaling proteins.
- **Phosphodiesters**: the backbone of DNA and RNA, and phospholipids.
- **Phosphoanhydrides**: the β-γ and α-β linkages of ATP, GTP and other NTPs.
- **Mixed anhydrides**: acyl phosphates such as 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.

**Why hydrolysis is so favorable.** Standard ΔG°' for ATP → ADP + Pi is about -30.5 kJ/mol. In cells it is roughly -50 to -60 kJ/mol, because [ATP]/[ADP][Pi] is held far from equilibrium. The driving forces are:
- **Electrostatic repulsion** between adjacent negatively charged phosphates, which is relieved on cleavage.
- **Resonance**: Pi has more equivalent resonance forms than the bound phosphate.
- **Solvation**: the products are better hydrated.
- **Ionization**: ADP releases H+ at pH 7, pulling the equilibrium forward.

**Kinetic stability.** Even though hydrolysis is strongly favorable, ATP is stable in water for hours to days. The negative charges repel incoming nucleophiles. This combination is ideal: ATP releases its energy only when an enzyme catalyzes the reaction.

**Mg2+ is essential.** Inside cells, ATP exists mainly as **Mg-ATP**. Mg2+ shields negative charge and fixes the conformation of the phosphate chain. This helps an enzyme aim a nucleophile at the correct phosphorus.

**Where nucleophiles attack:**
- **γ-P attack** gives ADP + a phosphorylated product. Kinases do this.
- **α-P attack** gives AMP + **pyrophosphate (PPi)**. This is used in fatty acid activation, amino acid activation by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and DNA polymerization. Pyrophosphatase then hydrolyzes PPi, making the overall process essentially irreversible.

**Phosphoryl transfer potential.** Phosphoenolpyruvate (-61.9 kJ/mol), 1,3-BPG (-49.4) and creatine phosphate (-43.1) rank above ATP. Glucose-6-phosphate (-13.8) ranks below. ATP's middle position lets it act as a shuttle between high-energy donors and low-energy acceptors.
levels.phd:
**Mechanism of phosphoryl transfer.** Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus spans a range of transition states. At one end is a **dissociative** (DN+AN) path with a metaphosphate-like, loose transition state. At the other is an **associative** (AN+DN) path through a pentacoordinate phosphorane intermediate. A concerted ANDN path lies between them. For phosphate monoester dianions, linear free-energy relationships point to a loose transition state. Kirby's studies of aryl phosphates found βlg near -1.2 and βnuc near 0.1-0.3, meaning large bond cleavage to the leaving group with little bond formation to the nucleophile. Diesters and triesters shift toward tighter, more associative transition states. In-line attack causes **inversion at phosphorus**. Knowles showed this using chiral [16O,17O,18O]-phosphoryl groups: each single displacement inverts, so net retention signals a phosphoenzyme intermediate (double displacement).

**Remarkable rate enhancements.** Wolfenden estimated the uncatalyzed half-life of phosphate monoester dianion hydrolysis at about 10^12 years at 25 °C. Phosphatases accelerate this by up to around 10^21-fold, among the largest catalytic proficiencies known.

**Westheimer's argument.** In "Why Nature Chose Phosphates" (1987), Westheimer argued that phosphate is uniquely suited to biology:
- It is trivalent, so it can link two nucleotides and still carry a negative charge.
- That charge keeps DNA inside membranes and resists hydrolysis.
- The charged esters still react under enzyme control.

Arsenate esters, for comparison, hydrolyze in minutes. This is one reason arsenate uncouples phosphorylation: ADP-arsenate forms and then falls apart by itself.

**Thermodynamics, revisited.** The "high-energy bond" (Lipmann's ~P) describes the system, not the bond. Breaking a P-O bond costs energy; the free energy released comes from the products being better stabilized. Measured ΔG of hydrolysis depends strongly on [Mg2+], pH and ionic strength. Alberty's transformed thermodynamics treats ATP as a sum of protonated and Mg-bound species.

**Enzymatic strategy.** Kinases use two Mg2+ ions, a conserved Lys and the glycine-rich loop to neutralize charge on the β/γ phosphates. Studies with transition-state analogs (AlF3/AlF4- and MgF3- complexes) support trigonal-bipyramidal geometry with apical nucleophile and leaving group. A catalytic Asp positions the substrate hydroxyl for attack on the γ-phosphate.
levels.expert:
**Pharmacology targets phosphoryl transfer directly.** About 80 small-molecule kinase inhibitors are now FDA-approved. Most are **type I** inhibitors, which mimic adenine and form hydrogen bonds to the kinase hinge. Imatinib is **type II**: it binds the inactive "DFG-out" conformation. Covalent inhibitors such as osimertinib (EGFR) and ibrutinib (BTK) carry an acrylamide that reacts with a non-catalytic cysteine near the ATP pocket. Allosteric agents like asciminib bind the BCR-ABL myristoyl pocket instead. Intracellular ATP is millimolar, so cellular potency often falls well short of biochemical IC50. This gap is a recurring pitfall when comparing inhibitors.

**Prodrug and nucleotide chemistry.** Phosphate charge blocks passive membrane crossing. Two strategies get around this:
- **Phosphate ester prodrugs**: fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug that alkaline phosphatases cleave back to phenytoin, avoiding the vehicle problems of IV phenytoin.
- **ProTide phosphoramidates**: sofosbuvir, tenofovir alafenamide and remdesivir mask the monophosphate with an aryl group and an amino acid ester. Inside the cell, esterases (cathepsin A, CES1) and HINT1 unmask it, bypassing the slow first phosphorylation step. Phosphorus is a stereocenter here, and single Sp diastereomers are chosen for activity.

**Bisphosphonates** replace the P-O-P oxygen with P-C-P. This makes them non-hydrolyzable pyrophosphate analogs that bind bone hydroxyapatite. Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as zoledronate inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts.

**Neuro relevance.** Neurons use a large share of ATP on the Na+/K+-ATPase, which works through an aspartyl-phosphate intermediate (a P-type ATPase). In ischemic stroke, ATP falls within minutes, pumps fail, and cells depolarize and swell (cytotoxic edema). In the penumbra, the creatine kinase/phosphocreatine buffer is used up first. ³¹P-MRS can track PCr, Pi and ATP noninvasively, and the chemical shift of Pi reports intracellular pH. Extracellular ATP also acts as a transmitter on P2X/P2Y receptors. Ectonucleotidases (CD39, CD73) degrade it to adenosine.

**Open questions.** Is the transition state for enzymatic phosphoryl transfer as loose as in solution, or does the enzyme tighten it? Vibrational and KIE data remain debated. Why do some kinases tolerate GTP? How can covalent inhibitors avoid resistance from cysteine mutations such as EGFR C797S?

keyPoints: ATP = adenine + ribose + α, β, γ phosphates
Phosphate esters are P-O-C; phosphoanhydrides are P-O-P
Hydrolysis is favorable due to repulsion relief, resonance and solvation
ATP is thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable
Mg2+ shields charge and orients ATP in enzymes
Attack at γ-P gives ADP; attack at α-P gives AMP + PPi

lessons.title: Nucleobases: Tautomers, Base Pairing and Chemical Damage

levels.kid:
Your DNA is like a giant instruction book written with only four letters: **A, T, G and C**. Each letter is a small ring-shaped molecule called a **base**.

The bases hold hands in pairs across the ladder of DNA. A holds hands with T. G holds hands with C. They fit like puzzle pieces, using tiny sticky spots called hydrogen bonds.

Sometimes a base changes its shape for a moment, like a puzzle piece that bends. Then it might grab the wrong partner, and a spelling mistake can happen.

Bases can also get damaged by sunlight, by certain chemicals, or just by water slowly nibbling at them. Luckily, your cells have repair crews that find broken letters and fix them.
levels.hs:
DNA and RNA store information using **nucleobases**: flat rings made of carbon and nitrogen. There are two families:
- **Purines** (two fused rings): adenine (A) and guanine (G).
- **Pyrimidines** (one ring): cytosine (C), thymine (T, in DNA) and uracil (U, in RNA).

In the double helix, bases pair by **hydrogen bonds**, weak attractions between an H on nitrogen and a lone pair on an O or N. This is called **Watson-Crick pairing**: A pairs with T using 2 hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C using 3. A purine always faces a pyrimidine, so the helix stays the same width.

Bases can exist as **tautomers**, which are forms that differ only in where a hydrogen atom and a double bond sit. The normal forms are the **keto** and **amino** forms. Rarely, a base flips into an **enol** or **imino** form. That changes its pattern of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, so it can mispair, which is one source of mutations.

Bases also suffer **chemical damage**. A real example: ultraviolet light in sunlight can fuse two neighbouring thymines into a **thymine dimer**. This kinks the DNA and blocks copying. Too little repair of these dimers raises skin cancer risk.
levels.college:
**Structure and aromaticity.** Purines (A, G) and pyrimidines (C, T, U) are planar, aromatic heterocycles. They attach to the sugar at C1' through a **β-N-glycosidic bond**: N9 in purines, N1 in pyrimidines. Ring nitrogens come in two kinds:
- **Pyridine-like N** has a lone pair in the ring plane. It acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and is weakly basic. Examples are N3 of cytosine and N1 of adenine.
- **Pyrrole-like N–H** donates its lone pair into the π system, so it acts as a hydrogen-bond donor.

**Tautomers.** The dominant forms in water are **lactam (keto)** and **amino**. Minor **lactim (enol)** and **imino** tautomers swap donor and acceptor positions. Watson and Crick's 1953 model only worked once Jerry Donohue pointed out that the keto forms of G and T are the correct ones. Rare tautomers allow mispairs such as G·T or A·C that mimic the Watson-Crick geometry. Watson and Crick proposed this as a mechanism of spontaneous mutation.

**Pairing and stacking.** G·C pairs form three hydrogen bonds and A·T pairs form two. Even so, **π-stacking** between neighbouring bases contributes much of duplex stability. That is why melting temperature (Tm) rises with GC content partly through stacking, not just hydrogen bonds.

**Major damage chemistry:**
- **Deamination:** cytosine is hydrolysed to uracil. 5-Methylcytosine deaminates to thymine, giving C→T transitions at CpG sites.
- **Depurination:** the N-glycosidic bond hydrolyses, leaving an **abasic (AP) site**.
- **Oxidation:** reactive oxygen species give **8-oxoguanine**, which pairs with A and causes G→T transversions.
- **Alkylation:** electrophiles attack nucleophilic N7 and O6 of guanine.
- **UV light:** [2+2] photocycloaddition gives **cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers** and **6-4 photoproducts**.

Cells counter these lesions with base excision repair (BER) for small lesions, nucleotide excision repair (NER) for bulky lesions, and direct reversal.
levels.phd:
**Tautomeric equilibria, quantitatively.** In aqueous solution, the canonical tautomers of the bases predominate by roughly 10^4–10^5:1. Minor enol or imino populations are estimated near 10^-4 to 10^-5. This sits intriguingly close to the intrinsic misincorporation rate of polymerases before proofreading. Classic Topal-Fresco models invoked rare tautomers for transitions. Al-Hashimi and colleagues used NMR relaxation dispersion (Kimsey et al., Nature 2015, 2018) to detect transient G·T and A·C Watson-Crick-like mispairs in duplex DNA. These form through tautomerization and through ionization, with populations around 0.1–1% within a wobble equilibrium. Crystal structures of polymerase active sites also show G·T mispairs adopting Watson-Crick geometry. This supports the idea that a tightly fitting active site can enforce rare forms.

**Nucleophilicity map.** The reactivity of guanine toward electrophiles follows N7 > O6 > N3, roughly. SN2 agents such as methyl methanesulfonate mainly give N7-methylguanine, which is weakly mutagenic but labilizes the glycosidic bond. SN1-type agents such as N-nitroso compounds alkylate the harder oxygen nucleophiles more. This yields the highly miscoding O6-methylguanine, which pairs with T. The correlation of O6/N7 ratio with the Swain-Scott s value is a textbook HSAB illustration.

**Hydrolytic instability.** Lindahl showed that DNA undergoes spontaneous decay, estimating about 10^4 depurinations per mammalian cell per day and roughly 100–500 cytosine deaminations. This work contributed to his 2015 Nobel Prize, shared with Modrich and Sancar. Depurination proceeds through an oxocarbenium-like transition state at C1'. N7-protonation or N7-alkylation of the purine enhances the leaving-group ability. 2'-Deoxyribose lacks the stabilizing inductive effect of 2'-OH, so DNA depurinates faster than RNA.

**Oxidation.** Hydroxyl radical and singlet oxygen target C8 of guanine, which has the lowest oxidation potential of the bases. The product, 8-oxo-dG, adopts the *syn* conformation and presents a Hoogsteen face to adenine. In guanine runs, electron holes migrate through stacked bases and localize on 5'-GG sites, as shown by Barton and Giese.

**Photochemistry.** Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers form from the singlet excited state on picosecond timescales. Dimer formation depends on stacking geometry at the moment of absorption. Femtosecond studies show that the bases' ultrafast internal conversion, which dissipates UV energy as heat, is itself a protective property.
levels.expert:
**Clinical exploitation of base chemistry.** Many anticancer and antiviral drugs are deliberate base mimics or base-damaging agents:
- **Temozolomide**, central in glioblastoma therapy, is a prodrug. It generates the methyldiazonium ion, which methylates N7-G, N3-A and O6-G. Cytotoxicity arises from O6-meG·T mispairs triggering futile mismatch repair cycles. The direct-reversal enzyme **MGMT** transfers the methyl group to its own cysteine in a suicide reaction. **MGMT promoter methylation**, which silences the gene, predicts benefit from temozolomide (Hegi et al., NEJM 2005). This makes it a routine neuro-oncology biomarker. Acquired resistance often follows mismatch repair loss, with a characteristic hypermutation signature.
- **5-Fluorouracil** and **6-mercaptopurine/thioguanine** exploit purine and pyrimidine recognition. Thiopurine toxicity varies with TPMT and NUDT15 genotype.
- **Mutagenic nucleosides:** molnupiravir's N4-hydroxycytidine tautomerizes between amino and imino forms. It pairs as C or U, driving viral error catastrophe. It is a direct pharmacological application of tautomer chemistry.
- **Cisplatin** crosslinks adjacent guanines at N7 (1,2-intrastrand GpG). Nucleotide excision repair capacity influences sensitivity.

**Mutational signatures.** Cancer genomics reads base chemistry directly. SBS1 reflects spontaneous 5-meC deamination at CpG and acts as a clock-like signature. SBS7 is UV signature, with C→T at dipyrimidines. SBS4 is tobacco-associated G→T, from bulky adducts. SBS11 reflects temozolomide exposure. APOBEC cytidine deaminase signatures (SBS2/13) show enzymatic deamination as an endogenous mutagen.

**Pitfalls.** 8-oxo-dG measurements were long inflated by artefactual oxidation during DNA isolation. ESCODD standardization lowered accepted baselines by orders of magnitude. In sequencing, deamination in FFPE (formalin-fixed) tissue produces spurious C→T calls, unless samples are UDG-treated.

**Frontiers.** Base editors (Komor and Liu, 2016) harness deaminases to install C→T or A→G changes without double-strand breaks. They are effectively engineered, targeted base damage. Open questions include how much spontaneous mutation truly stems from tautomers versus ionized bases or polymerase-enforced geometry. Another is how expanded alphabets (Romesberg's hydrophobic pairs, Benner's hachimoji DNA) show that pairing needs shape complementarity more than hydrogen bonds.

keyPoints: Purines (A, G) have two rings; pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one
Watson-Crick pairs: A·T with 2 H-bonds, G·C with 3
Keto/amino tautomers dominate; rare enol/imino forms can mispair
Base stacking contributes much of duplex stability
Damage: deamination, depurination, oxidation (8-oxoG), alkylation, UV dimers
Base chemistry underlies drugs like temozolomide and repair biomarkers like MGMT

test.q: Which nucleobase is a purine?
test.explain: Guanine and adenine are purines with two fused rings; C, T and U are single-ring pyrimidines.

test.q: How many hydrogen bonds hold a G·C Watson-Crick pair together?
test.explain: G·C forms three hydrogen bonds, while A·T forms two.

test.q: Tautomers of a base differ in the position of:
choices: A methyl group and an oxygen
A hydrogen atom and a double bond
A carbon atom and a ring
test.explain: Tautomers interconvert by moving a proton and shifting a double bond, as in keto vs enol forms.

test.q: Why can a rare enol or imino tautomer cause a mutation?
choices: It swaps its hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites
It converts the pyrimidine base into a purine
It breaks the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA
It cuts the bond linking the base to its sugar
test.explain: Swapped donor and acceptor positions let the base pair with the wrong partner, such as G with T.

test.q: Deamination of cytosine produces which base?
test.explain: Hydrolytic loss of the amino group turns cytosine into uracil; it is 5-methylcytosine that deaminates to thymine.

test.q: Hydrolysis of the N-glycosidic bond of a purine leaves:
test.explain: Depurination removes the base and leaves an abasic (AP) site on the sugar.

test.q: 8-Oxoguanine is mutagenic mainly because it pairs with:
test.explain: In the syn conformation, 8-oxoG pairs with A, which leads to G→T transversions.

test.q: Ultraviolet light commonly links two adjacent thymines to form a:
test.explain: A [2+2] photocycloaddition creates a cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer that kinks DNA.

test.q: Besides hydrogen bonds, a major source of DNA duplex stability is:
test.explain: Stacking interactions between neighbouring bases contribute much of the helix's stability.

test.q: What do we call the minor tautomer of guanine or thymine in which C=O becomes C–OH?
test.explain: The enol (lactim) form is rare; the keto (lactam) form dominates.

test.q: In DNA, a purine always pairs with a ___, keeping the helix width constant.
test.explain: Purine-pyrimidine pairing gives each base pair the same width.

test.q: Which gene's enzyme removes methyl groups from O6-methylguanine?
test.explain: MGMT directly reverses O6-methylguanine; silencing of its promoter predicts response to temozolomide.

kidTest.q: Which letter does A pair with in DNA?
kidTest.explain: A pairs with T, and G pairs with C.

kidTest.q: What holds the base pairs together?
kidTest.explain: Hydrogen bonds act like tiny sticky spots between partners.

kidTest.q: What can happen if a base briefly changes shape?
kidTest.explain: A shape change can make it pair wrongly, causing a spelling mistake.

kidTest.q: Which of these can damage DNA bases?
kidTest.explain: UV rays in sunlight can stick two bases together.

kidTest.q: G holds hands with which letter? (hint: one letter, after B)
kidTest.explain: G pairs with C.

advancedTest.q: SN1-type alkylating agents produce more O6-methylguanine than SN2 agents do. The best explanation is that:
choices: Reactive carbocation-like species favor harder oxygen nucleophiles
SN2 agents cross the nuclear membrane too slowly to react
SN1 agents hydrolyse the glycosidic bond first
O6 is the most nucleophilic site for soft electrophiles
advancedTest.explain: By HSAB reasoning, hard, carbocation-like electrophiles react more at hard O6, while SN2 agents prefer softer N7.

advancedTest.q: Why does N7-alkylation of guanine accelerate depurination?
choices: It stabilizes the deoxyribose ring against opening
It converts guanine into a pyrimidine-like ring
It makes the purine a better cationic leaving group
It forms a cross-link between two adjacent strands
advancedTest.explain: A positively charged N7-alkyl purine leaves more easily, favoring an oxocarbenium-like transition state at C1'.

advancedTest.q: A glioblastoma with an unmethylated MGMT promoter would be expected to:
choices: Respond better because MGMT is silenced
Lose mismatch repair before treatment begins
Show more O6-meG·T mispairs than other tumors
Repair temozolomide lesions and respond less well
advancedTest.explain: An unmethylated promoter means MGMT is expressed, so it removes O6-methyl groups and blunts temozolomide's effect.

advancedTest.q: A tumor genome shows many C→T changes at CpG sites that accumulate with age. The most likely chemistry is:
advancedTest.explain: 5-meC deaminates directly to thymine, producing clock-like CpG C→T changes (SBS1); UV dimers occur at dipyrimidines instead.
